title: Reference without copying: how to bring brand identity into motion
description: The first version of the carousel was correct but didn't look like Clint. How I used the website, Figma and Aura's brand system to extract a visual system, without copying screens.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: Aura and the agents that show up in this tutorial's carousel.

blocks.text: The first version of the carousel passed every test: perfect loop, sound at the right volume, everything on the beat. And still, when I looked at it, something was missing. Clint was missing. It was a dark, flat carousel that could have belonged to any SaaS.
This tutorial is about that second pass: how I took the brand identity and brought it into motion, without giving in to the temptation of copying screens. Shall we?
Gather the right sources

I used three sources. Screenshots of the hero and the conversation screen from the website. The website's Figma file, where I pulled the original images: 3D avatars, backgrounds, icons. And the Aura brand system document, which defines the symbol, the colors and how it can or can't be used.

A tip: the .fig file is a compressed package. You can open it and extract its images even without access to the Figma API. There were 717 images. I built numbered thumbnail sheets so I could calmly pick what was useful.
Extract the system, not the screen

Copying the website screen into the slide gives a poor result: small text, too much information, nothing moves. What I did was break the reference down into reusable pieces. Each piece became a class in a brand file that every slide loads.

Look at slide 5. Before, it had a metrics panel in the background that didn't explain anything, and a panel that said "Clint AI" when the right name is Aura. After, the data lives inside Aura's answer, as bars that grow on the beat. The information got bigger and clearer.
Respect the brand rules

Aura's brand system has explicit rules: the symbol doesn't rotate off its axis, doesn't become a single color, and the word Aura never gets a gradient inside the product. In the CTA pill I had the symbol spinning. I removed it and swapped it for a scale pulse. It seems like a detail, but it's the kind of thing the brand team spots from a mile away.

The same went for typography. I tested three options on the same slide: Sora, Poppins and Poppins Light. The final call was Sora for the text, Poppins Light for the step pills, with the Clint symbol in them. Labels like "Real Clint interface" moved from the mono font to Sora.
It was the critique that showed the brand was missing:
Step by step
Gather screenshots, the design file and the brand guide. Without a guide, the live website is the reference.
List the pieces: light or background, surface, badge shape, symbol, typography, one accent color.
Write each piece once, in a file shared by every slide.
Make a test slide in three variations and choose by looking at it at phone size.
Check the guide's don'ts before animating the symbol.

A good reference isn't the one you copy best. It's the one you understand so well that you can create a new screen that looks like it came from it. In the next tutorial I show the critique process that made me realize the first version wasn't good.
